4. Unbalanced designs

unbalanced-mixed.Rmd

Ecological data are rarely perfectly balanced. Sites disappear, sampling dates are missed, habitat combinations occur at different frequencies, and some blocks cannot contain every treatment. Imbalance changes both the comparison being estimated and which observations may be exchanged under the null.

distmer distinguishes two common cases:

  • unequal representation among fixed predictors is handled by an explicit Type I, II, or III hypothesis;
  • unequal replication within random or blocked units is handled on the experimental-unit scale, with permutations restricted to comparable units.

The formula remains familiar. The important work is identifying what was independently assigned or sampled.

Unequal fixed-factor combinations

The vegan::mite data contain 70 mite communities and environmental measurements. Dividing water content into three broad classes produces unequal representation across wetness and topographic classes.

data(mite, mite.env, package = "vegan")
mite_env <- transform(
  mite.env,
  Wetness = cut(
    WatrCont,
    breaks = quantile(WatrCont, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),
    include.lowest = TRUE,
    labels = c("dry", "intermediate", "wet")
  )
)
mite_env$Topo <- droplevels(mite_env$Topo)
mite_bray <- vegdist(mite, method = "bray")

cell_counts <- as.data.frame(table(mite_env$Wetness, mite_env$Topo))
names(cell_counts) <- c("Wetness", "Topography", "sites")
cell_counts  |> tab()
Wetness Topography sites
dry Blanket 10
intermediate Blanket 16
wet Blanket 18
dry Hummock 14
intermediate Hummock 7
wet Hummock 5 
ggplot(cell_counts, aes(Topography, Wetness, fill = sites)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sites), colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", direction = -1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "The environmental combinations are not equally represented",
       x = "Topography", y = "Wetness class", fill = "Sites")

For an additive ecological question, a Type II model compares each predictor after accounting for the other without making the result depend on formula order.

mite_fit <- permanova(
  mite_bray ~ Wetness + Topo,
  mite_env, type = "II", permutations = 999, seed = 17
)
mite_fit$table |> tab()
Source df SS MS Pseudo-F P(perm) P(MC) Unique perms
Wetness 2 2.168 1.084 7.002 0.001 0 999
Topo 1 1.136 1.136 7.337 0.001 0 999
Residual 66 10.215 0.155 NA NA NA NA
Total 69 14.696 NA NA NA NA NA

Use Type III only when an interaction is scientifically required and the requested effects are estimable. Empty cells or aliased columns are reported rather than converted into a different hypothesis. See vignette("fixed-effects") for the meaning of all three types.

Unequal repeated sampling

vegan::pyrifos follows aquatic-invertebrate communities in 12 experimental ditches over time. Dose was assigned to ditches, so the ditch—not each date—is the independent treatment unit. To illustrate missed visits, we retain between three and six dates per ditch, with every replication size represented in both treatment groups.

data(pyrifos, package = "vegan")
ditch <- gl(12, 1, length = nrow(pyrifos))
dose_by_ditch <- c(0.1, 0, 0, 0.9, 0, 44, 6, 0.1, 44, 0.9, 0, 6)
treatment_by_ditch <- factor(
  ifelse(dose_by_ditch == 0, "control", "exposed"),
  levels = c("control", "exposed")
)
visits_to_keep <- c(3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 6)
visit <- ave(seq_len(nrow(pyrifos)), ditch, FUN = seq_along)
keep <- visit <= visits_to_keep[ditch]

pyrifos_env <- data.frame(
  ditch = droplevels(ditch[keep]),
  treatment = treatment_by_ditch[ditch[keep]]
)
pyrifos_bray <- vegdist(pyrifos[keep, ], method = "bray")

ditch_summary <- data.frame(
  ditch = levels(pyrifos_env$ditch),
  treatment = unname(tapply(
    pyrifos_env$treatment, pyrifos_env$ditch,
    function(x) as.character(x[1])
  )),
  visits = as.integer(table(pyrifos_env$ditch))
)
ditch_summary$treatment <- factor(
  ditch_summary$treatment, levels = levels(treatment_by_ditch)
)
ggplot(ditch_summary, aes(ditch, visits, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_col(color="black", width = 0.75) +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:6, limits = c(0, 6.5)) +
  labs(title = "Unequal observation counts do not create extra ditches",
       x = "Ditch", y = "Retained visits", fill = "Group")

pyrifos_fit <- permanova(
  pyrifos_bray ~ treatment + (1 | ditch),
  pyrifos_env, permutations = 999, seed = 17
)
pyrifos_fit$table |> tab()
Source df SS MS Pseudo-F P(perm) P(MC) Unique perms
treatment 1 0.055 0.055 1.42 0.121 NA 999
Cluster-centroid Residual 10 0.391 0.039 NA NA NA NA 
pyrifos_fit$fit$test[
  c("estimand", "exchangeable_units", "permutation_strata")
] |> tab()

The comparison gives every ditch centroid equal weight, regardless of whether that ditch contributed three or six dates. Under the null, whole-ditch residuals move only among ditches with the same retained visit count. Treating all dates as independent would overstate replication and answer the wrong question.

The replication-size restriction must still permit treatment to vary. If, for example, every three-visit ditch were a control and every six-visit ditch were exposed, sampling effort and treatment would be confounded. distmer rejects that design because permutation cannot separate their effects.

Other forms of imbalance

The same experimental-unit principle extends to several field layouts:

  • ~ treatment + (1 | region/site) for unequal nested hierarchies;
  • ~ treatment + (1 | block) + (1 | treatment:block) for incomplete randomized blocks;
  • a crossed treatment plus (1 | region/site), (1 | treatment:region), and (1 | treatment:region:site) for crossed–nested studies;
  • predictors that vary among children or observations within a nested hierarchy.

For these models, complete units or treatment profiles move only within matching size or topology strata. Partly observed profiles, disconnected treatment incidence, zero denominators, and predictors confounded with strata are rejected. The random-effects guide explains the supported formula patterns and implementation choices in more detail.

Contrasts keep the same unit of evidence

Post-model contrasts must not fall back to observation-level replication. For supported mixed designs, permanova_mixed_contrasts() and permanova_mixed_pairwise() use the same unit-centroid estimand and restricted permutation structure as the overall model.

dose <- factor(rep(dose_by_ditch, 11)[keep])
contrast_env <- data.frame(ditch = pyrifos_env$ditch, dose = dose)
contrast_design <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ dose + (1 | ditch), contrast_env, pyrifos_bray
)
dose_levels <- levels(dose)
positive_vs_control <- setNames(
  ifelse(dose_levels == "0", -1, 1 / (length(dose_levels) - 1)),
  dose_levels
)

permanova_mixed_contrasts(
  contrast_design,
  contrasts = list(`mean positive dose - control` = positive_vs_control),
  permutations = 199, seed = 17
)$table |> tab()
contrast estimand df ss denominator denominator_df pseudo_f p_perm p_adjusted adjustment
mean positive dose - control mean positive dose - control equally weighted random-intercept unit centroids 1 0.055 MS[unit-centroid Residual] 7 1.565 0.145 0.145 holm

Checklist before fitting

  • Draw the sampling hierarchy and mark where each predictor varies.
  • Count observations within every experimental unit and treatment cell.
  • Decide whether groups, sites, or observations should receive equal weight.
  • Check that treatment varies within every required size or topology stratum.
  • State whether missingness is plausibly unrelated to the community response.
  • Report rejected or non-estimable comparisons rather than deleting the corresponding warnings.

Unbalanced inference can be defensible, but it cannot recover a treatment comparison that the sampling design never observed.
